title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Aerospace | MPI (US)
description: On-site magnetic particle inspection of aerospace steel parts, GSE and tooling for US manufacturers, suppliers and MROs, to your spec. Request an MT quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Aviation and Aerospace in the US
html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection (MPI) on ferromagnetic aerospace parts in the United States for manufacturers, suppliers, tooling shops and maintenance operations: high-strength steel forgings and machined fittings, fasteners and pins, landing-gear-type components, ground support equipment and tooling. Our technicians travel to your site and work to your specification and flow-down. For a quote, request an MT inspection quote and include the part list and the governing document.

Why magnetic particle inspection matters on aerospace steel

Aircraft use steel where strength and fatigue life matter most: landing gear cylinders and axles, wing and engine attachment fittings, actuator housings, bolts, shafts and bearing races. These parts operate at high stress with little margin, and a small surface crack can grow in a few thousand cycles. MPI finds those cracks. It works on carbon, low-alloy and many precipitation-hardening steels, it detects very fine, tight surface and near-surface cracks that other methods can miss, and the result is visible directly on the part.

The same strengths define the limit. MPI is for ferromagnetic material only, which excludes aluminum, titanium, most stainless grades and copper alloys; those parts go to liquid penetrant testing. And MPI shows only flaws at or just under the surface; internal discontinuities in forgings and bar are found by ultrasonic testing.

The rules and standards that apply

Aerospace MPI is rarely driven by a general construction code. Most often a purchase order or work instruction invokes a customer or prime process specification, and that document points to ASTM E1444 for the magnetic particle practice, with ASTM E709 as a general guide. Maintenance and alteration of US-registered aircraft are governed by 14 CFR Part 43, and certificated repair stations operate under 14 CFR Part 145. The people and stations holding that authority sign off airworthiness and return aircraft to service; Atlantis does not. When we examine a part for a manufacturer or repair station, our report goes into the customer's quality record and the customer decides disposition.

Technicians are qualified under the Atlantis written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A and aligned to the customer's flow-down. A Level II performs and interprets the examination; an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies, so if your quality system adds qualification steps for the examiner, tell us when you ask for a quote.

Parts and components suited to MPI

Typical candidates include steel forgings and machined fittings after final machining, bolts, studs and pins, bushings and shafts, and welded steel assemblies such as engine mounts and structural tubing. Ground support equipment, such as jacks, stands, towbars and lifting fixtures, has welded steel that cracks at connections under repeated loading. Tooling and assembly fixtures are another place where a fatigue crack can go unnoticed and then move a structure out of position. On those items our magnetic particle weld inspection technique is the same as in other industries, and the aerospace difference lies in the control of process, cleanliness and records.

Techniques that fit aerospace work

Because aerospace parts are mostly clean, machined and sometimes plated or coated, the wet fluorescent method with continuous magnetization is usual. Iron oxide particles suspended in an oil or water vehicle are applied while the field is on, and the part is examined under ultraviolet light in a darkened booth or area. The suspension concentration is checked with a settling test, and the ultraviolet intensity and ambient white light are measured against the limits in the governing process specification. Dry powder and visible-particle suspensions are used for rough or large parts, such as ground equipment, where a darkened area is impractical.

Magnetization method depends on the part. A head-shot or central conductor produces a circular field for finding longitudinal cracks in bars, pins and tubes; a coil shot produces a longitudinal field for finding transverse cracks. Complex parts need more than one shot so every area is seen in two directions. A portable AC yoke covers welds on tooling and GSE. Prods are normally prohibited on aerospace parts because arc strikes burn the surface and can start cracks in high-strength steel; the written procedure states what equipment is allowed.

Process control: cleaning, burn risk and demagnetizing

  • Cleaning: oil, grease, paint, rust and scale come off in the examination zone, using a method that does not harm the part or plating. Plated surfaces may be examined through the plating if the procedure allows it.
  • Contact points: electrical contact can arc on a dirty or painted surface. Copper contact pads and clean surfaces reduce it, and any burn is reported.
  • Field direction and strength: a field indicator or a part with known flaws verifies that the technique works before the production examination.
  • Demagnetizing: residual magnetism can attract particles or chips, disturb compass or instrument assemblies and affect later welding. The part is demagnetized and checked with a meter to the limit in the specification.
  • Post-cleaning: particles and suspension are removed after inspection, so nothing stays in oil passages or threads.

Planning around plant and maintenance schedules

Aerospace sites control access, parts movement and process steps. Expect to arrange visitor or contractor badging and a safety orientation, and in some facilities an export-control briefing. Wet fluorescent work needs a dark area, a power supply for the bench or portable unit, an exhaust path for vapors and a place for waste suspension. Parts in quarantine or waiting for release are examined in an order agreed with your quality department, and the date the report is due becomes part of the scope. If your site has its own booth and bench, tell us; we can bring only the consumables and the technician.

Plating and heat treatment sequence matters. High-strength steel may be examined before plating and after the final grind, depending on the specification, and grinding after heat treatment can produce cracks that only MT finds. Hold times between processes and the order of NDT steps are set by the customer document, and we follow them.

Reading indications: relevant, non-relevant and false

A clean aerospace part can still show particle buildup that is not a crack. A change in cross section, a keyway, a sharp thread root or the edge of a press fit can hold particles because the field leaks there by design; these are non-relevant indications and the technician identifies them by their location and by re-examining after remagnetizing. False indications come from poor cleaning, excess particles or a rough surface. A relevant indication is one caused by a discontinuity, such as a crack, a seam, a lap or a grinding check, and it is evaluated against the acceptance class. Grinding cracks look like a network of fine lines at right angles to the grind direction, and they are a classic finding on hardened steel that was overheated during machining.

The technician records what was seen, wipes the indication and, where the specification permits, repeats the test to confirm. Whether a part with a relevant indication is scrapped, reworked or sent to engineering for review is the customer's decision, as is any change of acceptance class.

Heat treatment, grinding and plating: where MPI falls in the sequence

Where the examination sits in the manufacturing sequence decides what it can catch. Quench cracks and heat-treat cracks appear after hardening, so an examination before heat treatment cannot see them. Grinding damage appears after the final grind. Plating and coating processes can hide fine cracks, and some processes introduce hydrogen that makes high-strength steel brittle, so the specification orders the steps and may require a bake. A part examined before plating and not again afterward carries a risk that the owner should understand. Our job is to follow the sequence on the customer's router or work instruction and record where in the sequence each examination happened, so the history of the part is clear if a question arises later.

For parts coming back from service, cleaning is the larger task. Hydraulic fluid, carbon deposits, sealant and corrosion products must come off the examination surface, and the cleaning method must not damage a plating or a protective finish. Disassembly, cleaning and reassembly are the customer's processes. We examine the clean part and report what we find.

What the report contains

The report identifies the customer, part number, serial or lot, drawing revision, material and condition. It states the governing specification and revision, the written procedure, the equipment and magnetization method, the particle material with lot or batch, the suspension concentration check, the ultraviolet and white light readings where used, and the demagnetization result. Each indication is recorded with location and size, with a sketch or photograph and an accept or reject decision against the stated limit. The technician, level and ASNT Level III reviewer are named, and any area that could not be examined is listed.

What to send for a quote

  • Part list with part numbers, material, condition and quantities
  • The specification, revision and acceptance requirements
  • Whether you will provide a bench, booth and power or need us to bring equipment
  • Site location, badging, export-control and safety requirements
  • Required report date and any hold or quarantine arrangements

Where we work in the US aerospace market

We mobilize to plants, tooling shops and maintenance sites in these regions, each with a dedicated MT page.

  • Wichita: airframe and business-jet supply chain with heavy steel and tooling work.
  • Seattle: Puget Sound structures suppliers and machine shops.
  • Hartford: engine and landing gear component manufacturing.
  • Charleston: aerostructure assembly and the suppliers around it.
  • Savannah: business aircraft production and support.
  • Fort Worth: military aircraft and rotorcraft suppliers.
  • Oklahoma City: maintenance depot and air logistics work.
  • San Antonio: aircraft maintenance and component overhaul.

Training your own technicians

For a plant that wants its own MT inspectors, Atlantis offers MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with the magnetic particle simulator for practice. We can also help write the employer's procedure through NDT procedure development. The employer certifies its personnel under SNT-TC-1A. For industry programs see aviation NDT training, and for the method in all industries see magnetic particle testing.

What we do not do here

Radiography is not something Atlantis performs in the United States. We do not examine composite structure, we do not offer specialist techniques on this page, and we do not sign off airworthiness or return aircraft to service. If your specification names an examiner qualification or an approval that Atlantis does not hold, we will tell you before any work is scheduled.

faq.q: Can you do magnetic particle inspection on aircraft landing gear parts?
faq.a: We examine ferromagnetic steel components to the customer's specification at the customer's site. The customer's repair station or quality system decides disposition and signs off airworthiness; Atlantis does not.

faq.q: Does MPI work on aluminum or titanium aircraft parts?
faq.a: No. Magnetic particle inspection needs a ferromagnetic material. Aluminum and titanium parts are examined for surface cracks with liquid penetrant testing, and for internal flaws with ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: Why are prods not used on aerospace steel?
faq.a: Prods can leave arc burns on the surface of high-strength steel, which can themselves start cracks. Aerospace procedures generally require coils, a central conductor or a yoke, and our written practice follows the specification.

Fine iron particles carrying a fluorescent dye are applied in a liquid while the part is magnetized. Under ultraviolet light, a crack shows as a bright line, which gives high sensitivity on clean, machined aerospace parts.

faq.q: Do parts have to be demagnetized afterward?
faq.a: Usually yes. Residual magnetism can attract debris, disturb nearby instruments and affect welding, so the specification sets a residual field limit that we verify with a meter and record.
The one in your purchase order or work instruction. It often points to ASTM E1444 for the process and sets acceptance classes. We apply its sensitivity, equipment and reporting requirements.

faq.q: Can you bring your own bench and booth?
faq.a: We can bring portable equipment for many jobs. For wet fluorescent work in a darkened area, tell us what the plant provides, since the booth, power supply and waste handling affect how we scope the work.

faq.q: What is the difference between MT and PT on an aircraft part?
faq.a: MT uses a magnetic field and works only on magnetic steel, showing surface and near-surface flaws. PT uses a liquid that enters surface-breaking cracks and works on nonmagnetic metals as well, but not on near-surface flaws.

faq.q: How are non-relevant indications handled on keyways and threads?
faq.a: The technician identifies them from their location and geometry, re-examines after remagnetizing where needed, and records them as non-relevant with a note. Anything doubtful is evaluated as a possible flaw until it is resolved.
